note: Source clause "as will be seen" dropped.
replacement: In Syracuse, meanwhile, reports of the expedition arrived from many quarters, but for a long time nobody believed them at all. An assembly was held, and different orators spoke, as will be seen, some trusting the report of the Athenian expedition and some contradicting it. Among them Hermocrates, son of Hermon, came forward. He was convinced that he knew the truth of the matter, and he gave the following counsel:

note: "may perhaps think" strengthened to "may well think".
replacement: “Let us therefore begin our preparations here with confidence. Let us send to some of the Sicels to confirm them, and win the friendship and alliance of others. Let us dispatch envoys to the rest of Sicily to show that the danger is common to all, and to Italy to get its cities to become our allies, or at any rate to refuse to receive the Athenians. I also think it would be best to send to Carthage as well. The Carthaginians are by no means free of apprehension; they live in constant fear that the Athenians may one day attack their city, and they may perhaps think that they themselves would suffer if Sicily were sacrificed. They may be willing to help us secretly if not openly, in one way if not in another. If they will, they are better able to do so than anyone alive today, since they possess the most gold and silver, by which war, like everything else, flourishes. Let us also send to Lacedaemon and Corinth, and ask them to come here and help us as soon as possible, and to keep the war in Hellas alive. But the one thing above all others that I believe we should do at this moment is something that you, with your constitutional love of quiet, will be slow to see, and that I must nevertheless mention. Suppose we Siceliots, all together, or at least as many as possible besides ourselves, were to launch our whole actual navy with two months’ provisions and meet the Athenians at Tarentum and the Iapygian promontory. Suppose we showed them that before fighting for Sicily they must first fight for their passage across the Ionian Sea. We should strike dismay into their army and set them thinking that we have a base for our defensive, since Tarentum is ready to receive us, while they have a wide sea to cross with all their armament. That armament could hardly keep its order through so long a voyage, and since it would come on slowly and in small detachments, it would be easy for us to attack. On the other hand, suppose they lightened their vessels, drew together their fast sailers, and attacked us with these. Then we could fall upon them when they were wearied with rowing, or, if we did not choose to do so, we could retire to Tarentum. They, having crossed with few provisions merely to give battle, would be hard put to it in desolate places. They would have either to remain and be blockaded, or to try to sail along the coast, abandoning the rest of their armament; and they would be further discouraged by not knowing for certain whether the cities would receive them. In my opinion this consideration alone would be enough to deter them from putting out from Corcyra. While they deliberated and reconnoitered our numbers and whereabouts, they would let the season run on until winter was upon them. Or, confounded by so unexpected a circumstance, they would break up the expedition, especially as their most experienced general, as I hear, has taken the command against his will, and would grasp at the first excuse offered by any serious demonstration of ours. We should also be reported, I am certain, as more numerous than we really are. Men’s minds are affected by what they hear; besides, those who are first to attack, or to show that they mean to defend themselves against an attack, inspire greater fear, because men see that they are ready for the emergency. This would be just the case with the Athenians at present. They are attacking us in the belief that we shall not resist, thinking they have a right to judge us severely because we did not help the Lacedaemonians in crushing them. But if they were to see us show a courage for which they are not prepared, they would be more dismayed by the surprise than they could ever be by our actual power. I could wish to persuade you to show this courage. But if that cannot be, at all events lose not a moment in preparing generally for the war. Remember, all of you, that contempt for an assailant is best shown by bravery in action, but that for the present the best course is to accept the preparations that fear inspires as the surest promise of safety, and to act as if the danger were real. That the Athenians are coming to attack us, that they are already on the voyage, and that they are all but here: of this I am sure.”
